entry.dc:title: HOW TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF THE NEW OSM BLASTING REGULATIONS.
entry.dc:creator: Ayat M.
entry.dc:description: The frequencies of blastwaves can at times disturb the more distant structures more than the nearer ones. To address such conditions, the Office of Surface Mining (OSM) recently completed new regulations designed to be more effective in preventing damage to structures in the vicinity of surface coal mines. Many operators are not taking advantage of the methods that OSM and the associated state regulatory authorities are now allowing; these methods are discussed.

entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd. have been offering almost all types of construction machinery. This paper particularly highlights typical machines used in coal surface mining. Moreover, the company is presently developing a superlarge hydraulic excavator based on the latest technology.

entry.dc:title: Geotechnical stability in surface mining. Proceedings of the international symposium, Calgary, 6-7 November 1986.
entry.dc:creator: Singhal R.K.
entry.prism:publicationName: Geotechnical Stability in Surface Mining Proceedings of the International Symposium Calgary 6 7 November 1986
entry.dc:description: The over 50 papers are concerned with on-going research and developments concerning the geotechnical stability of natural and man-made geo-structures implicated in surface mining. The main session themes are: surface mine design; design of pit wall slopes; drilling and blasting; slope excavation; artificial support; geotechnical stability-case histories; liquid storage and tailings pond; geotechnical properties; design of waste dumps; slope stability monitoring. Most of the papers are abstracted separately. -M.A.Bass

entry.dc:title: Rilling of hillslopes reclaimed before 1977 surface mining law, Dave Johnston Mine, Wyoming
entry.dc:creator: Soulliere E.
entry.dc:description: The erosion of hillslopes reclaimed following the surface‐mining of coal is an important geomorphologic concern. However, progress in the design of post‐mining topography and its hydrologic response has been hampered by the paucity of research focusing on the propensity of rill formation on these disturbed surfaces. This investigation is intended to partially rectify this situation through the development of regression equations for the prediction of rill frequency and magnitude based upon site characteristics. Rill width can be estimated using soil bulk density, hillslope age, and hillslope length with a standard error of 0.152 log<inf>10</inf> units at this location. Rill depth can be estimated using soil shear strength, hillslope length, and hillslope age with a standard error of 0.114 log<inf>10</inf> units. Rill length can be estimated using hillslope length, percent silt in the soil, hillslope age, Bouyoucos Clay Ratio, and soil bulk density with a standard error of 3.515 m. Rill frequency can be estimated using soil bulk density, Bouyoucos Clay Ratio, soil compaction, soil reaction (pH), and hillslope age with a standard error of 0.241 rills/m. The cross‐product of rill width times depth can be estimated using soil shear strength, hillslope length, hillslope age, and soil bulk density with a standard error of 0.260 log<inf>10</inf> units. These results must be tested further under various environmental conditions. Nevertheless, prediction of rill formation seems to be a problem capable of solution. entry.dc:title: Problems associated with rock material properties in surface mining equipment selection.
entry.dc:creator: Atkinson T.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions Institution of Mining Metallurgy Section A
entry.dc:description: Continuous mining systems may be split into 2 major sub-systems - excavation and haulage - in which characteristic problems occur. The main materials-related problems that affect both continuous and non-continuous surface mining operations are summarized. The factors that influence materials excavation and handling problems are discussed and index tests are presented that may be used to identify abrasive mineralogy and the physical properties of materials. The importance of materials testing both prior to equipment selection and during excavation is stressed and consideration is given to the integration of data on material properties into long- and short- term planning. -from Authors

entry.dc:title: Coal resources of the Tongue River member, Fort Union formation (Paleocene), Powder River Basin, Wyoming and Montana.
entry.dc:creator: Ayres W.
entry.prism:publicationName: Report of Investigations Geological Survey of Wyoming
entry.dc:description: The Tongue River member contains >1.16 X 10<sup>9</sup> short tons of low-sulphur subbituminous coal to a depth of 3000 ft in the Powder River Basin of Wyoming and Montana. Coal occurs in thick (commonly >60 ft), laterally extensive beds that have been correlated >50 miles along strike. In a regional subsurface study, data from 1790 geophysical well logs were used to map Tongue River coal beds and calculate resources for an area of 9651 sq ft at places in the centre of the basin. Much of the Powder River Basin's coal resources are contained in two thick strike-parallel coal beds. The first (commonly called the Wyodak coal bed) crops out along the E margin of the basin where it is exploited by surface mining; the second seam (identified as Seam 14 in this study) lies basinward (W) of the first at depths of 1000-2000 ft.-G.B.G.

entry.dc:title: Coal-mining technology in China
entry.dc:creator: Shen S.
entry.dc:description: Although China is the second largest coal-producing country in the world, the geological conditions of the country's coal seams are not always favorable. The coal seams in most of the existing coal-mining areas are to deep for surface mining. Therefore, about 96% of China's total coal production is from underground mines. Since the early 1950s great efforts have been made to improve coal-mining technology in China. The longwall retreating mining method has been popularized, and production from longwall faces account for about 92% of the total. About 40% of the total production is from thick coal seams using the slicing system. During the last 10 years the priority has been to improve the mechanization of longwall face operations. In the near future research will emphasize the development of new coal technologies for mining thin seams, extra thick seams, and steeply dipping seams. © 1986.

entry.dc:title: Chemical quality of suspended sediment from watersheds subjected to surface coal mining
entry.dc:creator: Dick W.
entry.dc:description: The chemical quality of suspended sediment in surface water runoff, which is changed as a result of surface coal activities, may influence water quality and have effects where the sediment is deposited downstream from the mine site. Suspended sediment samples were collected from three small watersheds in east-central Ohio prior to, during and after surface mining and reclamation. The chemical quality of the suspended sediment was determined by measuring Ca, Mg, Fe, Al, Mn, Ni, Pb, Cd, Cu, Zn, Sr, P (following pretreatment of the sample with 30% H<inf>2</inf>O<inf>2</inf> and extraction with 0.3 M HCl), acetate-soluble SO<inf>4</inf><sup>2-</sup>, pH, organic C, and Hg. Differences in concentrations of parameters were observed among the three watersheds and were related to the composition of the overburden material. At Watersheds C06 and M09, the concentrations of the chemical parameters in suspended sediment samples, collected after reclamation had been completed, were not significantly (P = 0.05) different than concentrations measured prior to surface mining. An exception was the concentration of organic C, which was lower during the postreclamation period. The concentrations of Mg, Fe, and Al were significantly greater at Watershed J11 during the postreclamation period compared to the premine period while P, organic C, Mn, and Pb concentrations were significantly lower. Concentrations of parameters in suspended sediment samples collected concurrently at the inlet and outlet of the sediment ponds at Watersheds C06 and M09 were not significantly (P = 0.05) different. However, due to settling of the larger and heavier sediment particles, a trend toward increased concentration of parameters in sediment samples collected at the pond outlet compared to the pond inlet occurred at both Watersheds C06 and M09.

entry.dc:title: BASIN WATER MONITORING: HYDROLOGIC IMPACT OR LEGAL COMPLIANCE
entry.dc:creator: Duckson D.
entry.prism:publicationName: Jawra Journal of the American Water Resources Association
entry.dc:description: ABSTRACT: The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (PL 95–87) requires data collection prior to mining which will allow a determination to be made of the probable hydrologic consequences. Modeling strategies exist which allow for such determination, but selection of a specific model form will dictate the length of data record needed. The absence of a sound management strategy by the regulatory authority in‘Maryland does not result in valid data collection and suggests that the agency is concerned more with legal compliance than with integrated resource management. entry.dc:title: Nickel, cadmium, and selenium levels in native soil, overburden, and spoil materials
entry.dc:creator: Pitt J.
entry.dc:description: Nickel (Ni), cadmium (Cd), and selenium (Se) analyses showed that there was no significant difference in the concentration of these elements when compared over the three sample types examined (native soil, overburden, and spoil materials obtained from four surface mining operations in Texas). The soils belong to the Paleustalf, Paleudult, Hapludalf, and Paleudalf Great Groups. Ranges in total concentrations of the individual elements were 4.01 to 71.4 mg kg<sup>-1</sup> Ni, 0.00 to 2.46 mg kg<sup>-1</sup> Cd, and 0.04 to 10.7 mg kg<sup>-1</sup> Se for the native soil, overburden, and spoil samples. At each site, the geological environments of deposition had significantly different levels of Ni, Cd, and Se. Depositional environments containing higher concentrations of fine materials (Backswamp, flood basin, etc.) had the highest concentrations of Ni and Cd. Selenium was highest in the lignite and deposits closely associated with the lignite. Results of this study indicate that no significant elevation of total Ni, Cd, and Se would be expected from the complete mixing of overburden following the surface mining operation.

entry.dc:title: SURFACE MINING: EQUIPMENT SELECTION AND USE ARE THE KEYS TO PROFITS.
entry.dc:creator: Singhal R.K.
entry.dc:description: A wide variety of equipment is used for material excavation in surface mining including scrapers, electric cable shovels, front-end loaders, hydraulic shovels, draglines, and bucketwheels. Various types of haulage trucks, conveyors, scrapers, trains, and pipelines are used for transporting the excavated material. The article examines selection factors.

entry.dc:title: Towards reducing the physical environmental impact of North American surface coal mines; a review of potential selective overburden handling techniques
entry.dc:creator: George H.
entry.dc:description: In North America, coal and lignite are presently extracted from natural materials by a variety of surface mining techniques that are largely dictated by factors such as coal thickness and attitude, overburden characteristics, and geological complexity of the deposit. Although a large variety of techniques are used, they are often similar within certain geographic regions, each being associated with a typical method of overburden handling and one or more major type(s) of physical environmental impact (topographic, stratigraphic and/or geohydrologic). While it is technically feasible to modify current routine overburden handling practice, or to introduce effective novel selective handling techniques in order to reduce subsequent environmental damage within each geographic region, economic factors do not always favour selective methods. Because of the possibility of increased stripping costs, the implementation of any selective overburden placement scheme requires site-specific appraisal of the profitability of the operation. In some situations, however, the use of selective techniques in place of conventional methods can actually be economically superior. The appropriate selective overburden placement schemes that can be applied in the different geographic regions are assessed in this review. © 1986 Elesevier Science Publishers B.V.

entry.dc:title: EVALUATING WHEEL LOADERS AND FRONT SHOVELS.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: The availability of hydraulic front shovels in the 10- to 12-yd**3 class increases the number of large loading machines for surface mining. Although both the wheel loader and front shovel have distinct advantages, and each can often handle the work of the other, the economics are different. Manufacturers of front shovels often claim their machines are a better choice in tough digging applications because of high breakout forces and faster cycle times. Although the hydraulic shovel cycled faster, the wheel loader had a significant advantage in the amount of overburden moved per bucket load. The result, the wheel loader uncovered 2700 st more coal per eight-hour shift - a 30% production advantage. Even when comparing a 13-yd**3 front shovel to a 13. 5-yd**3 wheel loader, which Caterpillar did in a more recent study, the advantage still goes to the wheel loader.

entry.dc:title: COMMERCIALIZATION OF EASTERN US OIL SHALES - A REVIEW.
entry.dc:creator: Rajaram V.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions of the American Institute of Mining Metallurgical and Petroleum Engineers Society
entry.dc:description: The oil shales located in the Appalachian Basin cover an eight-state area of the eastern US and are referred to as Devonian (black) shales. These shales have been exploited for their gas potential for several years. The Institute of Gas Technology (IGT) has conducted research since 1972 on the production of shale oil from the Devonian shales. This resulted in the development of the HYTORT process. This process demonstrated that the yield from the Eastern oil shales can be greater than the value indicated by the Fischer assay method. IGT estimates that 67 Gm**3 (423 billion bbl) of oil could be recovered by HYTORT processing of surface minable eastern US shales. Recently, American Syncrude Corp. and Southern Pacific Petroleum NL have proposed oil shale projects in Kentucky. This paper will describe the surface mining and retorting techniques that have been studied for exploitation of the Devonian shales, and enumerate the problems that have to be overcome before commercial production can be realized.

entry.dc:title: RELATION BETWEEN GROUND-WATER QUALITY AND MINERALOGY IN THE COAL-PRODUCING NORTON FORMATION OF BUCHANAN COUNTY, VIRGINIA.
entry.dc:creator: Powell J.
entry.prism:publicationName: US Geological Survey Water Supply Paper
entry.dc:description: Core material from the Norton Formation of the Pennsylvania Period is composed of slightly more than one-half sandstone; siltstone and minor amounts of shale, clay, and coal account for the majority of the remainder. Petrographic analyses and x-ray diffraction studies indicate that the sandstone is about 75 percent quartz, 15 percent plagioclase feldspar, 2 percent potassium feldspar, 2 percent plagioclase feldspar, 2 percent potassium feldspar, 2 percent muscovite, 4 percent chlorite, and 1 percent siderite. No limestone strata were identified. Three reaction models are used to account for the observed water chemistry. The models derive sulfate from pyrite, iron from pyrite and siderite, calcium from plagioclase and calcite, sodium from plagioclase and cation exchange, magnesium from chlorite, and carbon from carbon dioxide, calcite, and siderite. Kaolinite, chalcedony, and goethite are formed authigenically. Carbon-13 data define the relative contributions of carbon sources to models. Comparison of adjacent unmined and mined basins indicates that surface mining significantly increases the weathering reaction of pyrite in contrast to weathering reactions of other minerals. Refs.

entry.dc:title: Marsh community development in a central Florida phosphate surface-mined reclaimed wetland
entry.dc:creator: Erwin K.L.
entry.dc:description: As the nation's acreage of productive freshwater marsh/wetlands continues to decrease the need for sucessful marsh restoration/reclamation increases. A variety of land uses including surface mining, residential development and agriculture create direct impacts on wetlands often resulting in a net loss of habitat if appropriate restoration or reclamation of the ecosystem is not obtained within a reasonable period of time. The 30 hectare freshwater marsh reclaimed from a phosphate mined area is part of a 148 hectare upland, 61 hectare wetland ecosystem (Agrico Swamp) reclaimed in 1981/82. Topsoil additions have been a successful means of establishing a marsh system within the site. This technique shows distinct advantages over natural revegetation of overburden. At the end of two full growing seasons the topsoiled area has higher species richness and cover values than the overburden areas. During this period a slight decline in the species richness in the topsoiled area was evident due in part to the aggressive nature of Pontederiacordata. Conversely, the species richness of the overburden areas increased significantly. Topsoiling appears to encourage the accelerated establisment of late successional plants in sufficient quantities to compete with aggressive weedy species such as Typhalatifolia. © 1985 Society of Wetland Scientists.

entry.dc:title: BUCKAU WOLF SURFACE MINING EQUIPMENT IN NEYVELI LIGNITE MINES IN INDIA.
entry.dc:creator: Raybarman P.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels

The lignite field at Neyveli is spread over approximately 100 sq miles with an estimated range of 2000 million tonnes. Continuous mining technology as used in German mines has been adopted.

entry.dc:title: DEVELOPMENT OF BUCKET WHEEL EXCAVATOR.
entry.dc:creator: De A.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of the Institution of Engineers India Mining Engineering Division
entry.dc:description: Bucket wheel excavator is an important equipment for surface mining projects, which are used in lignite mines throughout the world. The concept and its application are more than 100 years old. The machine has been modified on several occasions to suit project conditions. Important changes are the modifications of buckets, cell chutes, bucket driving units, travel mechanisms, luffing arrangements, and counter weight structures. This paper presents these and the latest techniques that have been incorporated in a systematic way.

entry.dc:title: SEDIMENT YIELD AND WATER QUALITY FROM A STEEP-SLOPE SURFACE MINE SPOIL.
entry.dc:creator: Dickens P.S.
entry.prism:publicationName: Transactions of the American Society of Agricultural Engineers
entry.dc:description: Sediment yield and storm runoff water quality from a steep-slope, back-to-contour, coal surface mining spoil in the New River Basin of Tennessee were monitored for a period of three years. Sediment and mineral constituent concentrations observed in storm runoff from the spoil increased to a maximum 1. 1 to 1. 3 years following the completion of mining, then declined. This increase was associated with the loss of mulch provided at reclamation and the onset of rill and gully erosion. Maximum sediment yield also occurred within this period. By the end of the third year following mining, a dense and uniform vegetative cover had become established on the spoil.

entry.dc:title: PRODUCTIVITY FROM BUCKET WHEEL EXCAVATORS.
entry.dc:creator: Golosinski T.
entry.dc:description: The continuous mining systems as used in surface mining operations consist of four main components: the bucket wheel excavators (BWE) to dig the material, conveyors to transport the material from the excavator to the spreader, trippers for the transport of the material from conveyor to the spreader, and spreaders to dump the material. The production rate of a BWE depends on several factors: the design and operating parameters of a BWE; the geomechanical properties of materials to be mined; the design of cuts and the geometry of the mining face; the performance and reliability of other components of the mining system; and the organization of work. The estimated yearly BWE system productivity should be verified against the performance of similar existing BWE operations.

entry.dc:title: SUCCESS OF COMPACT BWE'S IN GREECE EYED BY U. S. MINES.
entry.dc:creator: Chironis N.
entry.dc:description: Surface mining is basically an earth-moving operation and the ideal way to move earth is by some continuous excavating and conveying method. This is why in Europe, South Africa, Australia, Canada and, in fact, most of the surface mines outside of the United States, the bucket wheel excavator (BWE) is the chief tool for overburden excavation as well as coal loading. The article reviews applications in several countries.

entry.dc:title: SINKING SHAFTS FOR OIL: TWO BOLD NEW VENTURES BEGIN.
entry.dc:creator: Anon
entry.dc:description: Devran Petroleum and Shell Canada Resources have a 6. 3 million project near Sarnia, Ont, which is expected to recover up to 2 million barrels of oil that was left in place when conventional recovery methods were exhausted in the early 1900s. Utilizing a system that was developed in the 1930s, Devran as operator will sink a shaft, construct two production stations within the petroleum bearing strata, and drill a radial pattern of horizontal production wells. Another project concerns oil sands which the Alberta government is funding under the auspices of Aostra, its research arm devoted to evaluating techniques for recovering bitumen from the vast portion of the oil sands not accessible by surface mining.
